business_flow: The traffic shows a user interacting with a web application: visiting root, login/logout, forgot-password flow including a temporary token, viewing posts (/post?postId=4) and a user account page (/my-account?id=wiener). Several static/resource endpoints are requested. No API endpoints with JSON bodies were present. Actions include GET and POST to /forgot-password and POST to /login. The session cookie is present in many requests.
thought_process: I examined each of the 21 HAR entries and applied the five checks (IDOR/BLA9, State Manipulation/BLA3, Sequence Bypass/BLA6, Shadow Endpoints/BLA10, Internal Disclosure/BLA8) to each endpoint.

Only endpoints that expose business-relevant parameters or tokens (query parameters or form flows) can meaningfully contain BLVs under the provided framework. Static resources and simple root fetches that return 0 (no response captured) or only static content rarely show BLVs in this trace.

I will report findings only where the traffic shows potential business logic weaknesses (e.g., direct object references in URLs without proof of ownership enforcement, temporary forgot-password token usage surfaced in querystring, and user account endpoint accepting an id parameter). For each such finding I produce a separate PoC with payload mutation and a curl using placeholders as required.

potential_vulnerabilities.description: GET /my-account?id=wiener accepts a user identifier in the query string. This is a direct object reference that may allow an attacker to view another user's account by changing the 'id' parameter to another username (IDOR) if server-side ownership/authorization checks are missing. Evidence: the request includes an id parameter and returns 200 for id=wiener.

reproduction_guide.payload_mutation: Change query parameter 'id' from 'wiener' to another username (e.g., 'carlos' or '{{target_id}}') to attempt viewing another user's account.

potential_vulnerabilities.description: GET /forgot-password?temp-forgot-password-token=dkq281bj0r4y481a7f7t6hurpsf4ru9k exposes a temporary forgot-password token in the URL query string. Inclusion of a sensitive token in a GET query can lead to token leakage via logs, referer headers, or browser history (internal state disclosure). The presence of the token in the captured request indicates the token is used as a URL parameter.

reproduction_guide.payload_mutation: Use the exposed 'temp-forgot-password-token' value directly in the URL. Example: change token to another known/guessed token '{{target_id}}' or replay the same token to access the reset page.

potential_vulnerabilities.description: POST /forgot-password?temp-forgot-password-token=dkq281bj0r4y481a7f7t6hurpsf4ru9k returns a 302 and indicates the reset flow can be driven via the temp-forgot-password-token parameter in the URL. If the application does not validate that the token is tied to the current session or perform other ownership checks, an attacker could bypass normal email verification by supplying a valid token directly (workflow order bypass / sequence bypass). Evidence: entries show both GET and POST using the temp-forgot-password-token parameter and the POST returned 302 (likely performing reset).

reproduction_guide.payload_mutation: Send a POST to the forgot-password endpoint with the temp token in the URL (change token value to target token '{{target_id}}'). If the application accepts any valid token regardless of session binding, this will perform the reset without original email/flow context.
